Home labs

Two labs I built and still run

One practices the analyst's job: investigate, document, escalate. The other practices the infrastructure that analysts defend.

SOC LAB · VIRTUALBOX, FLAREVM, REMNUX · RUNNING SINCE SEPTEMBER 2026

Investigated a SQL injection attack and Cerber ransomware in Splunk, then took apart real malware samples and phishing emails

I work through the SOC analyst's loop in a virtual lab: triage alerts in Splunk, analyze phishing emails and live malware samples, check endpoint and network evidence, and write the findings down. My notes cover phishing, SIEM, Windows, Linux, and malware analysis exercises.

Splunk SPLSuricata alertsFlareVMREMnuxANY.RUNVirusTotalMITRE ATT&CKWiresharktcpdumpSysmonINetSimWindows Event Logs
See what I did
  • Phishing

    Worked two phishing email samples in FlareVM. Pasted the headers into MXToolbox, where SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all failed, and read the last "Received from" hop to find the true sender behind four hops. In the first, the verify-payment link was a link shortener, so I used ANY.RUN to see the real site. It blocked me with anti-analysis checks, so I routed through a Tor exit node, read the DNS requests to find the hosting domain, and VirusTotal flagged it 13/91. In the second, VirusTotal flagged the link 18/91 and urlscan.io showed an Excel-branded credential-harvesting login page.

  • SIEM

    Investigation 1, on the BOTSv1 dataset: narrowed a suspect IP (40.80.148.42) down to HTTP traffic against a web server (imreallynotbatman.com). POST requests carried "select" and "sleep" keywords in the form data, which is a SQL injection pattern. Suricata alerts split 46% web application attack, 18% network trojan, 14% attempted information leak. An SPL search surfaced 8 events containing the password attempts, and a second search found 2 executable requests, one of which (3791.exe) succeeded with a 200 and appeared in 69 Sysmon events. Investigation 2: starting from an alert on host we8105desk, Suricata flagged Cerber ransomware, and traffic between two internal hosts showed lateral spread. I exported the logs to CSV for incident reporting and configured a Splunk forwarder from FlareVM to my REMnux Splunk server.

  • Static

    Sample 1, RemcosRAT from MalwareBazaar: renamed with a trailing underscore so it could not run, hashed it with PowerShell, pulled strings with FLOSS (webcam, keylogger, and file-transfer functions, plus "Remcos" itself), and found 113 flagged imports in PeStudio. VirusTotal flagged it 64/72 with tags for dormancy and environment checks. Sample 2, a trojan posing as BraveUpdate: FLOSS surfaced "Enigma Protector", PeStudio measured entropy at 7.976 and a virtual size larger than the raw size, and Detect It Easy confirmed the packer. VirusTotal scored it 58/71 and its behavior tab showed masquerading and sandbox evasion.

  • Dynamic

    Detonated Remcos in FlareVM with INetSim running on REMnux and watched TCPView, ProcMon, and Regshot. Regshot showed 5 new keys, 5 new values, and 8 modified values. INetSim logs revealed a domain being contacted every three seconds, which is beaconing. VirusTotal flagged the domain as malicious, and its certificate was a short-lived 3-month Let's Encrypt one. On the packed trojan, the local tools showed nothing, which fit the packing finding, and ANY.RUN exposed the PowerShell commands it ran. I generated the ANY.RUN report for documentation.

  • Endpoint

    Learned the Windows evidence trail: Security, System, Application, and Setup logs. Generated failed logons (Event 4625) and compared them with my successful admin logon (4624 and 4672). Installed Sysmon, cleared its log, created a dummy malware file, and found two new Process Create events: Notepad launched by explorer.exe (human action) and then the calculator. Created a registry Run-key persistence example and mapped parent and child processes in PowerShell. Fixed a multi-layer RDP failure caused by VirtualBox networking, a static IP, and a Terminal Services misconfiguration.

  • Linux

    Reviewed the files an investigator checks (/etc/passwd, shadow, group, sudoers, crontab, and the auth and syslog logs). Wrote a script simulating C2 beaconing to a listener on my REMnux host on port 9999, verified the connection from both ends with Test-NetConnection and the listener's connect log, and captured it with tcpdump for Wireshark. Practiced cron persistence with a sample cron job.

  • Playbook

    Wrote an incident response playbook for phishing-induced malware with C2 activity. Containment steps: block the sender and C2 at the email gateway, firewall, and DNS filter, purge the email from all mailboxes, isolate the host, and reset credentials and revoke sessions. Then lateral-movement checks with Windows Event 4624 logon types 3 and 10 and Sysmon Event 3, hash blocking, and persistence removal.

ACTIVE DIRECTORY LAB · WINDOWS SERVER 2025 · VMWARE WORKSTATION PRO · RUNNING SINCE SEPTEMBER 2026

Built a redundant Windows domain and fixed a firewall and DNS replication failure

A two-controller domain with Group Policy, scoped admin rights, and a tested backup and recovery. When replication between the controllers broke, I traced it to the firewall and DNS, fixed it, and documented the fix.

AD DSDNSGroup PolicyFSMO rolesRAID1Least privilege
See what I did
  • Build

    Deployed Windows Server 2025 as a domain controller with AD DS, DNS, and Group Policy Management. Built four organizational units and managed user accounts, with password policy, account lifecycle, and logon restrictions.

  • Resilience

    Added a second domain controller with AD replication, cross-server DNS failover, and FSMO role distribution. Put the AD database on RAID1 and ran a full Active Directory backup and recovery.

  • Fix

    Diagnosed and resolved a firewall and DNS replication failure between the two servers without outside help.

  • Access

    Delegated password-reset-only control to a Help Desk role, following least-privilege principles. Set up security and distribution groups, shared folder permissions, and roaming profiles on domain-joined clients, plus a domain-joined print server with department-targeted Group Policy.

Method

How I work a phishing email

The steps I followed on a phishing sample in my SOC lab, in the order I ran them. After triage, my playbook moves to scoping, blocking, and cleanup.

  1. Read the headersSPF, DKIM, and DMARC results in MXToolbox.
  2. Trace the senderFollow the message across hops to find where it started.
  3. Unwrap the linkDe-obfuscate the shortened URL before opening anything.
  4. Detonate safelyOpen the site in ANY.RUN, with Tor routing for the one that resisted analysis.
  5. Confirm the domainCheck the hosting domain in VirusTotal and write it up.

BSides Orlando 2026

Two workshops · AI Red Teaming CTF · Red Team Tradecraft

In the CTF I attacked a deliberately vulnerable AI art studio across five levels: prompt injection, broken authorization, incomplete input filtering, output-channel blindness, and metadata leakage. The last level ended in CyberChef, decoding a base64 string left in image provenance data. The tradecraft workshop covered scoping an authorized red team engagement with the Physical Red Team Framework and documenting site reconnaissance.

Each of the five levels was a classic application security flaw wearing an AI costume.
